A1.justification: Despite renaming Any360D to PanDA and extensive revisions, both describe the same panoramic-depth research built around teacher–student learning, LoRA and Möbius augmentation. The text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation and transformation experiments, trained teacher/student results, and loss, architecture and augmentation ablations, including appendix experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original PanDA results on Matterport3D and Stanford2D3D, camera-position experiments, and extensive component and sensitivity analyses in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The teacher–student framework remains, but v1's DAM v1 adaptation with metric-depth heads and SILog-based objectives becomes DAM v2 adaptation producing normalized affine-invariant depths. v2 introduces equator-aware patch normalization loss, equator-biased sampling with boundary continuity, and gradient loss in supervised and pseudo-label training (Section 4).

E1.justification: Teacher training moves from real indoor Matterport3D to synthetic indoor Structured3D and outdoor Deep360. The stated unlabeled training set replaces self-collected Diverse360 with 360+x while retaining ZInD. v2 adds Stanford2D3D evaluation and controlled camera-height/location scenarios (Sections 3.2 and 5; Appendix A).

E2.justification: The Matterport3D comparison drops OmniFusion and adds BiFuse, BiFuse++, HoHoNet, HRDFuse, S2Net, Elite360D and Depth Anywhere (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 5). v2 also introduces quantitative zero-shot comparisons against DAM v1, DAM v2 and Marigold, and evaluates RPNL against EPNL.

E3.justification: v2 separates aligned zero-shot PanDA evaluation from unaligned, 30-epoch dataset fine-tuning, adds threshold-accuracy metrics and evaluation resizing, and changes student training from 20/40 epochs to four. Default training zoom expands from 1–1.2 to 1–1.5. DAM robustness testing expands from three rotation/zoom settings each to ranges of −90°–90° and 0.4–4.0.

E4.justification: v2 adds local-output representation analysis, controlled camera placement, EPNL/RPNL and equator/pole comparisons, pseudo-label-only training, limited-label fine-tuning, LoRA-rank sensitivity, and pseudo-label-resolution analysis. Existing loss, data-volume and augmentation-range ablations use revised designs. The metric-head comparison in v1 Table 5 is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix E.8 newly states that inference timings are averaged over 100 measurements; v1 has no corresponding procedure. Neither version reports repeated training runs, training seeds, or uncertainty intervals for depth-accuracy results.

E6.justification: DAM v1 representation RMSE values remain unchanged, but method results are substantially replaced and extended. v1 Table 3 reports student Matterport3D RMSE 0.3931; v2 Table 5 reports PanDA-S/L values 0.3950/0.3305, and Table 6 adds Stanford2D3D results, including PanDA-L RMSE 0.2540. Changed training and evaluation prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal definitions of percentile depth normalization and the patch-normalized EPNL objective (Equations 1–3). The spherical projections, Möbius transformation and inverse-projection mathematics are retained from v1 Appendix C.1 in v2 Appendix D.3. No new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

C1.justification: The claimed first comprehensive benchmark becomes a three-factor empirical analysis covering both DAM generations. v2 adds EPNL-based equatorial accuracy and synthetic indoor/outdoor joint training to its central contribution narrative, replacing v1's emphasis on metric-depth supervision and newly collected data. The broader SSL/MTSA generalization claim remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes disparity supervision and metric-head tradeoffs when explaining equatorial failures. v2 develops explanations involving global normalization, polar-region dominance and equator-focused supervision. Appendix E.6 newly acknowledges that visualization normalization can conceal DAM details; Appendix A identifies extremely dark scenes as problematic. Limited labeled-scene coverage remains a stated limitation.

D1.justification: v2 documents dataset-specific scaling/clipping, frame extraction and dark-scene filtering, sky masking, doubled-resolution pseudo-label generation, representation patch/FoV settings, EPNL sampling, LoRA rank, and inference hardware/timing. These substantially expand reproducibility information. v1's Diverse360 collection procedure and metric-head implementation details disappear with those components.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes its approach from Depth Anywhere's unlabeled-panorama distillation and positions EPNL relative to Metric3D's random patch normalization. DAM v2 and synthetic-data training become central reference points, while Marigold and diffusion-based depth estimation enter the discussion. This substantially revises the closest-work positioning beyond citation updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, analysis and methodology are extensively rewritten. The five-aspect benchmark becomes a three-factor analysis, experiments are organized around zero-shot and dataset-specific evaluation, and appendices become separate supplementary sections A–F. Any360D is renamed PanDA, with accompanying terminology and author-header changes.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening demonstration and pipeline, introduces transformation curves, camera-position illustrations, error maps and point clouds, and restructures comparison tables by dataset and evaluation setting. Large appendix image galleries are removed. Retained Möbius geometry material moves into the supplement rather than constituting a new analysis.

improvement.justification: v1's generalization evidence beyond Matterport3D is mainly qualitative. v2 substantially strengthens it through separate quantitative zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluations on two real datasets, plus EPNL/RPNL and equator/pole controls. Appendix E.6 also addresses a visualization confound. Outdoor accuracy and training variability remain unquantified, and zero-shot scores require scale/shift alignment, but the more diagnostic evidence and clearer protocols provide a substantial net improvement.
